extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in analytic number theory and the Riemann hypothesis
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic survey of the Riemann hypothesis: its formal statement, analytic background (zeta function, analytic continuation, functional equation), consequences for primes and arithmetic functions, equivalent criteria, generalizations, proven analogues, numerical verifications, and related conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the Riemann hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The real part of every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function is 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, the hypothesis states that all the nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line, consisting of the complex numbers 1/2 + it where t is a real number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and analytic continuation of the Riemann zeta function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Riemann zeta function is defined for complex s with real part greater than 1 by the absolutely convergent series ζ(s)=∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^s and Euler product ζ(s)=∏_{p prime} 1/(1-p^{-s}), and it must be analytically continued (meromorphically) to make sense over the complex plane (except a simple pole at s=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To discuss zeros outside the original domain of convergence one uses analytic continuation (via the Dirichlet eta relation and the functional equation). The functional equation ζ(s)=2^s π^{s-1} sin(π s/2) Γ(1-s) ζ(1-s) lets one define ζ(s) for Re(s)≤0 (with the simple pole at s=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivial vs nontrivial zeros and the critical strip/line
rubrics_metrics.description: Trivial zeros occur at the negative even integers (−2,−4,−6,…). Nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1; the Riemann hypothesis concerns whether all nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line Re(s)=1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The functional equation implies there are no zeros with negative real part other than the trivial zeros; nontrivial zeros are symmetric about the critical line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann's explicit formula linking zeros to prime distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Riemann's explicit formula expresses π(x) (or Π_0(x)) in terms of the logarithmic integral li(x) minus a sum over the nontrivial zeros li(x^ρ) plus other terms; the zeros control the oscillations of primes about their expected positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summation over zeros is evaluated in order of increasing absolute value of imaginary part. Care is needed defining li(x^ρ) because li has branch points at 0 and 1 (use analytic continuation/Ei). This connection motivates the importance of the location of zeros for prime distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for the prime-counting function (error bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If β is the upper bound of the real parts of the zeros, then π(x) − li(x) = O(x^β log x); in particular, the Riemann hypothesis (β = 1/2) implies strong error bounds such as π(x) − li(x) = O(x^{1/2} log x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Koch and Schoenfeld give explicit bounds: e.g., RH implies |π(x) − li(x)| < (1/(8π)) √x log x for all x ≥ 2657, and analogous bounds for ψ(x). Many practical consequences for prime gaps and explicit estimates follow from these bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth bounds for arithmetic functions (Möbius / Mertens equivalences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 1/ζ(s) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ μ(n)/n^s converges for every s with Re(s) > 1/2 (equivalently RH) is equivalent to bounds on the Mertens function M(x)=∑_{n≤x} μ(n), namely M(x) = O(x^{1/2+ε}) for every ε>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various improvements and conditional results exist (Soundararajan's conditional bound). The Mertens conjecture (|M(x)| ≤ √x) was disproved; RH is equivalent to a weaker growth condition on M(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindelöf hypothesis and implications for zeta growth
rubrics_metrics.description: RH implies the Lindelöf hypothesis: for any ε>0, ζ(1/2 + it) = O(t^ε) as t→∞, giving sharp bounds for the growth of ζ on the critical line and other regions of the critical strip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under RH one obtains precise limsup bounds for |ζ(1+it)| and for 1/|ζ(1+it)| in terms of log log t, up to constant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime gap bounds under RH (Cramér-type result)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, Cramér proved every gap between a prime p and its successor is O(√p log p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bound is far weaker than Cramér's conjectured O((log p)^2) gaps; numerical evidence supports stronger conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic criteria equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (Riesz, Hardy–Littlewood, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several analytic statements are equivalent to RH, e.g., the Riesz criterion: −∑_{k=1}^∞ ((−x)^k/((k−1)! ζ(2k))) = O(x^{1/4+ε}) for all ε>0 iff RH; the Hardy–Littlewood criterion and others provide alternate formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences often rephrase RH as growth or approximation properties of certain functions or series and have been used to study RH from varied analytic perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nyman–Beurling (and Báez-Duarte) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: RH is true iff the space of functions of the form f(x)=∑_{ν=1}^n c_ν ρ(θ_ν/x) (with ρ fractional part, 0 ≤ θ_ν ≤ 1 and ∑ c_ν θ_ν = 0) is dense in L^2(0,1). Báez-Duarte strengthened this to θ_ν ∈ {1/k}_{k≥1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This translates RH into a density/approximation problem in a function space (L^p variants give information about zeros to the right of 1/2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salem's integral equation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: RH is equivalent to the statement that the integral equation ∫_0^∞ z^{−σ−1} φ(z)/(e^{x/z}+1) dz = 0 has no non-trivial bounded solutions φ for 1/2 < σ < 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another reformulation expressing RH as a uniqueness/no-solution condition for a certain integral equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weil's and Li's positivity criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Weil's criterion states positivity of a certain function is equivalent to RH; Li's criterion states positivity of a certain sequence of numbers is equivalent to RH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give discrete or operator-theoretic positivity conditions equivalent to RH and are used in attempts to transform RH into verifiable inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speiser's criterion (zeros of ζ' and simplicity of zeros)
rubrics_metrics.description: RH is equivalent to the derivative ζ′(s) having no zeros in the strip 0 < Re(s) < 1/2. Moreover, ζ having only simple zeros on the critical line is equivalent to ζ′ having no zeros on the critical line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects the location and multiplicity of zeros of ζ and its derivative, offering a geometric perspective on RH.

rubrics_metrics.name: de Bruijn–Newman constant and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Define H(λ,z) via a family parameterized by λ; RH is equivalent to all zeros of H(0,z) being real, which is equivalent to the conjecture Λ ≤ 0 where Λ is the de Bruijn–Newman constant. Rodgers & Tao proved Λ ≥ 0, so RH is equivalent to Λ = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constant Λ gives a quantitative measure: proving Λ ≤ 0 (equivalently Λ = 0 using known lower bound) would prove RH. Current upper bounds (as of April 2020) give Λ ≤ 0.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH) for Dirichlet and other L-functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The generalized RH extends the conjecture to Dirichlet L-functions (and more generally to global L-functions), predicting that nontrivial zeros of these L-functions have real part 1/2; extended/ grand RH extend further to Dedekind/Hecke/automorphic L-functions and Selberg class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many consequences in algebraic number theory and analytic number theory use GRH. A proof method for the classical RH might plausibly extend to these broader classes, but GRH remains open as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and applications of GRH
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming GRH yields many conditional results: completeness of Gauss's class-number list, weak ternary Goldbach, bounds on first primes in arithmetic progressions, Artin's primitive root conjecture consequences, sharper estimates for discriminants and class numbers, polynomial-time primality tests via Miller, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some results originally proved using GRH were later proved unconditionally but were harder; many explicit number-theoretic theorems are known under GRH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proven analogues (function fields, Weil conjectures, Selberg/Ihara zeta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogues of RH have been proved in other settings: Weil proved the RH for curves over finite fields (leading to Deligne's proof of the Weil conjectures); Selberg proved analogous statements for Selberg zeta functions of Riemann surfaces; Ihara zeta functions relate to Ramanujan graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proven analogues motivate optimism and provide frameworks (e.g., spectral interpretations) that inform approaches to the classical RH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random matrix / Montgomery pair correlation connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture posits that correlation functions of suitably normalized zeta zeros match those of eigenvalues of random hermitian matrices; numerical evidence (Odlyzko) supports this connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statistical connection underlies many modern heuristics about zeros (GUE distribution), and Montgomery showed (assuming RH) at least 2/3 of zeros are simple; conjectures expect all zeros are simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical verification and zero computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive numerical computations verify that many zeros lie on the critical line and that RH holds up to large heights (e.g., Platt & Trudgian showed RH true up to 3·10^12 as of 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computational verifications support RH but do not prove it; computations also inform statistical investigations like pair correlation and testing of conjectures like simplicity of zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded-middle phenomena and theorems true either way
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theorems follow regardless of whether (G)RH is true or false (examples in Hecke/Deuring/Mordell/Heilbronn discussion); authors warn to specify which class of Dirichlet series one means when asserting GRH is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care is needed interpreting dichotomous theorems: some results are proved by separate arguments in the RH-true and RH-false cases, giving unconditional conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences involving elementary arithmetic functions (Robin, Lagarias, Franel–Landau, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many equivalences of RH with inequalities about arithmetic functions: Robin's theorem connects RH with σ(n) < e^γ n log log n for all n > 5040; Lagarias gave an equivalent inequality involving σ(n) and harmonic numbers; Franel–Landau equivalences relate RH to regularity of Farey sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences recast RH as explicit arithmetic inequalities, giving concrete (sometimes computationally checkable) conditions equivalent to RH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of zeros and connections to other L-functions (Dedekind, Artin, elliptic curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedekind zeta functions and some L-functions can have multiple zeros (e.g., due to factorization into Artin L-functions). For elliptic-curve L-functions, multiple zeros at the central point relate to the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity behavior in general L-functions shows that analogues of RH must be considered in broader contexts where simple-zero expectations may fail.
